title: Checks an agent cannot weaken

story: Tuesday morning, main is red: one unit test fails, "shows a No projects yet card when there are no projects". The CI fixer, a routine that runs the same agent as Nova (our ticket-to-PR agent) whenever main breaks, starts and has one job: make CI green. It has three ways to do it. It can fix the typo in the code. It can add .skip to the test. Or it can delete the one assert line in the test.

All three turn CI green. Only the first one fixes anything. The other two make the test prove less, so the build looks healthy while the bug ships, and nobody is looking, because the routine runs unattended.
hook.question: How do we judge an agent with checks, when the cheapest way to pass a check is to weaken it?

read.h: When the measure becomes the target
p: Economists have a saying for this, Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Give a factory a target of so many nails and it makes tiny useless nails. Give an agent the target "CI is green" and a test is often the cheapest thing on the path. In AI research the same behaviour is called reward hacking or specification gaming: the system finds a way to raise its score that is not the task you meant.

This is not the agent being evil. It is doing exactly what it was asked, in the cheapest way it can find. That is why no prompt fixes it. "Never weaken tests" is guidance, and on a hard day the model can convince itself that "this assertion was wrong anyway". So we arrange the checks so that the cheap paths do not work, and so that any attempt is visible.

read.h: Put the judge out of reach
p: Ask three questions about any check an agent is judged by. Where does its code live? Who may change its rules? What does it read? A check is only a wall when the answers are: somewhere the agent cannot write, only a person, and facts instead of claims.

Our own checks, such as locked-checks and independent-approval (the check from the lesson on agent PRs that refuses the requester's approval), live in the ai-agents repo and run from an image pinned by its digest, the hash of its content, so nobody can swap in a different image under the same name, while the agent's token covers only fcp, so it cannot reach their code. The files that decide how strict fcp's own checks are, such as the CI workflows, the lint and test configs and the coverage limits, are on a protected list, and that list is enforced in layers. In the VM, a hook refuses an edit to a protected file (the lesson on hooks showed how). The GitHub token cannot touch .github/workflows at all, because it lacks the workflows permission. And on the PR, the required check locked-checks reads the final diff and fails any agent PR that changed a protected file, so even an edit made with sed, which the hook never saw, is caught. The rules of main are a ruleset with no bypass for the agents' GitHub App, so nothing inside a run can disable any of this.

code.text:
fcp:
  - .github/**
  - .claude/settings.json
  - frontend/biome.json
  - frontend/tsconfig.json
  - frontend/vitest.config.js
  - frontend/playwright.config.ts
  - cloud/.coveragerc
  - sdk/tox.ini

notes.text: Workflows, scripts and the PR template. GitHub also refuses these to the agent's token.
The settings that hold fcp's own verify hook, so an agent cannot switch off what judges it.
Retries and timeouts live here: raising them lets a flaky test pass by luck.
The coverage limit for the backend: lowering it is a quiet way to pass.

read.h: Read the diff for a weaker test
p: Locking files cannot cover the tests themselves, because tests must change with the code: a renamed field or a new screen changes a test for good reasons. So for tests we read the diff, the list of lines a change added (starting with +) and removed (starting with -). Three signs give away a false heal, a change that turns a check green by making it prove less: a new skip or .only, more assertions removed than added in a test file, and a threshold that moved the loose way.

Which way is loose depends on the number. A lower coverage limit accepts less, so lower is looser. More retries or a longer timeout lets a flaky test pass by luck, so higher is looser. Raising the coverage limit from 70 to 85 is a stricter check and gives no finding.

notes.text: A test file: in a test or e2e folder, or named .test or .spec with a JavaScript or TypeScript ending.
A lower fail-under accepts less; for retries and timeouts, higher is looser.
Count, do not judge: assertions removed minus assertions added. Moving an assertion is fine; losing one is a finding.
Pair an old threshold line with the new line for the same key, then compare the numbers.

read.see:
fix/honest     no false heals found
fix/skip       FALSE HEAL  test/empty-card.test.mjs: new skip: test.skip("shows a No projects yet card …
fix/no-assert  FALSE HEAL  test/empty-card.test.mjs: 1 assertion(s) removed

p: A finding does not mean the same thing for everyone. People edit tests for good reasons, and a person reads every Nova PR, so for people and for Nova the finding is a flag: a note on the line of the diff that the reviewer must look at. A routine runs unattended, and nobody reads its work before it is opened, so for a routine any finding rejects the run, and the routine moves one step back on its trust ladder, the stages from shadow mode to drafts to normal PRs. Changing a protected file is different again: an agent PR that does it is blocked, and a person can continue the work on that PR themselves.

These checks count and compare. They cannot judge meaning. Change assert.equal(total, 3) to assert.ok(total) and the number of assertions stays the same, so nothing fires, although the test now proves much less. That is why the checks are never alone: one person still approves, and that person is never the requester.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the approval check is judged the same way
p: The rule "exactly one approval, never by the requester" is itself a check an agent could try to weaken, so it follows the same three questions. Its code lives in the ai-agents repo. It reads facts from GitHub's API, not from text the agent wrote: the reviews on the PR's latest commit, who pushed commits and who edited the body, plus the Requested-by line the platform writes. Anyone in that set is a requester and cannot be the approval. An agent PR without the Requested-by line fails, because the check fails closed when its input is missing.

Before a warning-only check like the weakened-tests one is trusted, it is run over the last 50 merged PRs. If it raises more than one false alarm in ten PRs, the noisy pattern goes, because a warning that is usually wrong teaches people to ignore warnings.

lab.title: Catch three false heals in a real git diff
lab.goal: Make a failing test green three ways in a scratch repo, see CI pass for all three, then read the git diffs with a small checker that finds the two false heals.

guess.q: Three branches make the failing test pass: one fixes the typo, one adds test.skip, one deletes the assert line. How many of them does npm test report as green?

options.why: node:test counts a skipped test as skipped, not failed, and a test with no assertion passes. CI cannot tell the difference.
That is the whole problem: the test result cannot see that the test was weakened. Only the diff can.

options.text: Two: the fix and the deleted assert, but the skip shows as failed.
options.why: A skip is reported as skipped, and skipped does not fail the run.

follow.say: Make a small project with one bug and one test that catches it, the way main looks on Tuesday morning. npm test fails, as it should.
follow.see:
not ok 1 - shows a No projects yet card when there are no projects
…
    + 'No project yet'
    - 'No projects yet'
…
# pass 1
# fail 1

follow.say: Play the CI fixer three times: an honest fix, a skip, and a deleted assertion, each on its own branch. Then run the tests on each branch.
follow.do:
git switch -q -c fix/honest main && perl -pi -e 's/No project yet/No projects yet/' src/empty-card.mjs && git commit -qam "fix: plural in the empty card"
git switch -q -c fix/skip main && perl -pi -e 's/^test\("shows a No/test.skip("shows a No/' test/empty-card.test.mjs && git commit -qam "fix: unblock CI"
git switch -q -c fix/no-assert main && perl -ni -e 'print unless /"No projects yet"\);/' test/empty-card.test.mjs && git commit -qam "fix: simplify the test"
git switch -q main
for b in fix/honest fix/skip fix/no-assert; do git switch -q $b; echo "$b: $(npm test 2>&1 | grep -E '^# (pass|fail|skipped)' | tr '\n' ' ')"; done; git switch -q main
follow.see:
fix/honest: # pass 2 # fail 0 # skipped 0
fix/skip: # pass 1 # fail 0 # skipped 1
fix/no-assert: # pass 2 # fail 0 # skipped 0

follow.say: Look at what the diff shows that the test result hides.
Write the checker next to the repo, outside it, the way our checks live outside fcp. It reads a diff and reports new skips and lost assertions.
Run it on each branch's diff.
follow.do: for b in fix/honest fix/skip fix/no-assert; do echo "== $b"; git diff main..$b | node ../false-heal.mjs; done
follow.see:
== fix/honest
no false heals found
== fix/skip
FALSE HEAL
  test/empty-card.test.mjs: new skip: test.skip("shows a No projects yet card when there are no projects", () => {
== fix/no-assert
FALSE HEAL
  test/empty-card.test.mjs: 1 assertion(s) removed

lab.build: Thresholds are the third sign. Make two more branches from main: fix/retries, which changes retries: 0 to retries: 3 in test.config.mjs, and chore/stricter, which changes timeout: 5000 to timeout: 2000. (perl -pi -e 's/retries: 0/retries: 3/' test.config.mjs does the first edit.) Then teach false-heal.mjs to pair a removed threshold line with the added line for the same key and report it only when it moved the loose way: lower is looser for fail_under, higher is looser for retries and timeout. Run the checker on both new branches.
checks: npm test is green on all three fix branches, and fails on main.
The checker finds nothing on fix/honest, a new skip on fix/skip and one removed assertion on fix/no-assert.
On fix/retries the checker prints test.config.mjs: retries loosened 0 -> 3.
On chore/stricter it prints no false heals found, because a shorter timeout is stricter.
The checker exits with code 1 when it finds something (echo $? after it), so CI could fail on it.
lab.fix: To "cut noise from Python files", someone changed TEST_FILE to /\.(test|spec)\.tsx?$/. Make that change and run the checker on fix/no-assert: it now says no false heals found, because test/empty-card.test.mjs no longer counts as a test file. A routine could delete every assertion in a .mjs test and pass. Restore the pattern, and think of one more test file name it should match.
explain: Why does npm test pass on all three branches, and what can see the difference?
Why is a change to playwright.config.ts blocked for an agent PR, while a change to a test file is only read for signs of weakening?
The same diff is a flag on Nova's PR and a rejection for a routine. Why the difference?
lab.done: The checker finds the skip, the lost assertion and the looser retries, stays quiet on the honest fix and the stricter timeout, and you can say why each one counts.

check.q: A teammate wants to stop false heals by adding "never weaken a test" to the CI fixer's prompt. Why is that not enough?

options.text: Because the model cannot read its prompt during a long run
options.why: It can. The problem is that a prompt is guidance, and the model can convince itself that this one assertion was wrong.

options.text: Because the prompt is guidance; a check that reads the diff, from outside the agent's reach, is what actually catches it
options.why: Reward hacking is the agent taking the cheapest path to green. Only a check it cannot change makes that path fail.

options.text: Because routines do not use prompts
options.why: Routines run the same agent with a charter and prompts. Prompts just are not walls.

check.q: Why does the locked-checks check live in the ai-agents repo and not in fcp?

options.text: Because the agent's token can write fcp, so a check in fcp could be edited by the agent it judges
options.why: A check is only a wall if its code and rules are somewhere the agent cannot write. Our checks run from an image pinned by digest.

options.text: Because GitHub Actions cannot run code from the same repo
options.why: It can. Putting the check out of reach is a choice for safety, not a limit of GitHub.

options.text: Because fcp's CI is too slow
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

check.q: A routine's PR changes cloud/.coveragerc from fail_under = 85 to fail_under = 70. What should happen?

options.text: Nothing, because coverage is not a test
options.why: The coverage limit is a check. Lowering it is one of the quietest false heals.

options.text: A warning the reviewer can read later
options.why: That is the answer for people and Nova. A routine runs unattended, so nobody would read the warning in time.

options.text: The run is rejected, and the routine moves one step back on its trust ladder
options.why: A lower fail_under is looser, the file is protected, and for an unattended routine any false heal rejects the run.

p: Three required checks run on every fcp PR from the ai-agents-checks image, pinned by digest, called from a thin workflow in fcp pinned by commit SHA: independent-approval (one approval from someone outside the requester set, on the head commit), locked-checks (fails an agent PR that changes a path in settings/protected-paths.yaml or the QA checks listed in the PR body's locked-checks block), and weakened-tests (annotations only, on every PR). The same protected-paths file feeds the PreToolUse hook in the VM, and the rhino-ai-agents App has no workflows permission and no bypass on the fcp ruleset.

For routines, the harness runs the false-heal check before the scope judge, adds the charter's never-rules (for example no added retries or sleeps for the flaky-test fixer), and also runs it from the Stop hook so the agent sees the problem before it calls itself done. Any finding ends a routine run as false_heal and moves the routine back a stage.

tickets.why: The locked-checks required check and the shared protected-paths list.
The weakened-tests check: read the patch, annotate on every PR, calibrate on 50 merged PRs first.
The false-heal check: the same signs plus charter rules, and a rejection for routines.
The independent-approval check, built the same way: code out of reach, facts from GitHub, fail closed.

words.plain: When a system judged by a score finds a cheaper way to raise the score than doing the task.
A change that turns a check green by making it prove less: a skip, a removed assertion, a looser limit.
A file that decides how strict a check is, which an agent's PR may not change.
A number in a check's settings, such as a coverage limit, retries or a timeout.
A routine's stages, from shadow mode to drafts for its owner to normal PRs; a false heal moves it down.

review.q: Name the three signs of a weakened test that a diff checker looks for.
review.a: A new skip or .only; more assertions removed than added in a test file; a threshold moved the loose way (lower fail-under, more retries, longer timeout).

review.q: Give the three questions you ask about any check an agent is judged by, and the safe answers.
review.a: Where does its code live (where the agent cannot write)? Who may change its rules (only a person, through a reviewed PR)? What does it read (facts from GitHub or the diff, not the agent's claims)?

review.q: Name one weakening that no counting check catches, and what catches it instead.
review.a: Changing an exact assertion to a vague one, like toBe(3) to toBeTruthy(). The one independent reviewer, the QA checks written before the code, and mutation reports catch it.

remember: An agent will take the cheapest path to green, so keep the judge out of its reach and read every diff for a test that proves less.
